svg.text: Kernel depth, layer by layer — the receipt for the split
A kernel that is only half as deep as the previous layer can physically see only its own GPU. Read the third column and the split reads itself.

g.data-tip: Kernel depth 3 is the full RGB image, so both halves see the same input. The 96 kernels are simply dealt 48 to each card.
Depth 48 is exactly half of conv 1's 96 maps. The kernel cannot reach the other card's half even in principle.
Depth 256 is every conv 2 map on both cards. The only convolutional layer whose kernels read across the link, and the paper calls the choice of pattern a problem for cross-validation.
Back to half depth: 192 of conv 3's 384 maps. The streams separate again one layer after they met.
Half depth again: 192 of conv 4's 384 maps. conv 3, 4 and 5 run back to back with no pooling or normalisation between them.
Fully connected means connected to all neurons of the previous layer, so all three classifier layers exchange activations across both cards every forward and backward pass.
g.text: every neuron of the layer before

svg.text: Why two cards at all — and what the split was worth
More data lets a bigger net train without severe overfitting; 1.2M examples sufficed for nets too big for one 3 GB GTX 580.
Half the kernels live on each card. At conv 3 and fc 6–8 the GPUs read one another's memory directly, without going through host memory.
Reported gain: 1.7% top-1 / 1.2% top-5 vs a one-GPU net with half the kernels per conv layer, except its last conv and fc layers (footnote 2).
Two biases pull opposite ways: the larger-than-half baseline makes 1.7% understate the two-GPU net's gain, while twice the kernels
make it overstate what the split itself buys. Net reading: 1.7% is the gain of a bigger net, not of the split topology.
